sections.heading: Teach me to hold on to you
sections.text: Lord Jesus, teach me to love you and cling to you. I don’t want to keep embracing the sins and cravings I once held so tightly. You are better than what has trapped me, and I need you to make my heart believe that and live like it.
theological_themes: Love for Christ is a gift of grace, not merely an act of human will.
Repentance includes turning from beloved sins to embrace Christ as better.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes coming to see Christ as surpassingly valuable compared with everything he once treasured. That supports the prayer’s movement from clinging to sin toward embracing Christ as the true treasure.
Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him. The request to be given love for Christ rests on dependence on Christ rather than self-generated devotion.

sections.heading: You loved me before I loved you
sections.text: You loved me first, when I was not looking for you. I was your enemy, guilty and unclean, with nothing in myself to recommend me. When I had no good defense and could not even rescue myself, you claimed me as your own. You love me as your child, and when I wander, you do not shrug it off—you grieve over me with holy compassion.
theological_themes: Christ’s love comes before the believer’s response.
Grace reaches enemies and sinners, not the already worthy.
Adoption gives the believer a real place as God’s child.
Christ’s compassion is not indifference toward sin but grieving mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds salvation in Christ’s love for the ungodly and for enemies. This directly supports the prayer’s confession that Christ loved before there was any love or worthiness in the sinner.
This passage connects the Son’s redeeming work with adoption as sons and heirs. It supports the prayer’s confidence that Christ does not merely pardon but brings the believer into the family.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem’s refusal and coming judgment, showing that his love includes real sorrow over sin and unbelief. The prayer applies that revealed compassion personally, without making Christ indifferent to wandering.

sections.heading: The road your love took
sections.text: Your love did not stay at a distance. Love brought you down into our world. Love carried you to the cross and into the grave. Love made you willing to know tiredness, hunger, temptation, mockery, lashes, blows, spit, nails, and the spear. Love led you all the way to the moment when you bowed your head and died.
theological_themes: The incarnation and humiliation of Christ reveal divine love in action.
Christ truly entered human weakness and suffering without sin.
The cross is the climactic demonstration of Christ’s self-giving love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Son’s descent from divine glory into servant-form and obedience to death on a cross. This is the biblical shape behind the prayer’s movement from heaven to earth to crucifixion.
Hebrews teaches that Jesus was truly tempted as we are, yet without sin. That grounds the prayer’s mention of Christ entering human weakness and temptation.
John records Jesus’ thirst, death, and pierced side. This passage anchors the concrete sufferings named in the prayer in the Gospel account of the crucifixion.

sections.heading: You welcome me with joy
sections.text: My salvation is where your true human love and your eternal divine love meet in one Savior. You do not receive me like someone who is only painfully putting up with me. You welcome me with love and with joy. You are not cold, moody, or unreliable toward me. Even my stubbornness has not exhausted your mercy.
theological_themes: In Christ, fully God and fully man, saving love is both truly human and truly divine.
Christ welcomes repentant sinners gladly, not reluctantly.
The love of Christ is steadfast and not defeated by the believer’s remaining sin.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews explains that the Son shared our humanity in order to save and help his people. This supports the prayer’s careful claim that Christ’s saving love is truly human as well as divine.

In Jesus’ parable, the returning son is met with embrace, restoration, and celebration. That gives biblical shape to the prayer’s confidence that God welcomes repentant sinners with joy, not mere tolerance.
Paul declares that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ. This supports the prayer’s claim that Christ’s love is not intermittent or changeable.

sections.heading: Let your love make me holy
sections.text: Let your love light a holy fire in me by your Spirit. Make my obedience grow out of your mercy, not out of pride or fear. Since every spark of real holiness comes from you, turn my heart back toward you again and again, until what you begin in me burns brighter and stronger.
theological_themes: Holiness is the fruit of God’s love and the Spirit’s work.
Sanctification is not self-improvement for self-glory but a return to God, the source of holiness.
The believer’s obedience is sustained by grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes believers being transformed as they behold the Lord’s glory, and he attributes that transformation to the Spirit. This supports the prayer’s request for holiness kindled by divine love and carried on by the Spirit.
The fruit of the Spirit includes love and the character that flows from God’s work within the believer. This grounds the prayer’s dependence on the Spirit for a holy life.
Grace does not merely pardon; it trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live in holiness. That supports the prayer’s link between being loved by Christ and being changed by him.

sections.heading: Help me notice your love everywhere
sections.text: Open my eyes to your love, not only at the cross, but also among your people and in the world you have made. When I feel the warmth of the sun, help me praise you, the one whose righteousness rises with healing. When rain softens the ground, remind me how your gospel refreshes my dry soul. When I walk beside a river, lift my mind to the river of life in your city, where your people are made clean and given the right to the tree of life. Your love is deeper than I can understand, and my forever-rest will be to enjoy that love without end.
theological_themes: The cross is the central revelation of Christ’s love, but creation and fellowship can also become reminders of his goodness.
God’s ordinary gifts can lead the believer into worship when received with faith.
Christian hope ends in eternal life with God, cleansed and satisfied by his love.

scripture_references.connection: Paul prays that believers, together with the saints, would grasp the vastness of Christ’s love. This supports the prayer’s desire to see Christ’s love in the fellowship of believers, not only in private reflection.
Malachi uses the image of the sun of righteousness rising with healing, which the prayer draws on when turning the warmth of the sun into praise for Christ’s healing righteousness.

John’s vision of the river of life and the tree of life grounds the prayer’s river imagery in the promised eternal city. It points from an earthly river to the believer’s final hope in God’s presence.
This passage speaks of the redeemed whose robes are made white in the blood of the Lamb. It supports the prayer’s hope of being cleansed and welcomed into eternal life through Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original phrase describing the speaker as a “loathsome worm” reflects a severe Puritan idiom of self-abasement. I preserved the doctrine of deep sin and unworthiness while avoiding language that could imply God regards his adopted child as less than human.

The line about Christ weeping over the believer “as over Jerusalem” is a devotional application of Luke 19 rather than a direct biblical statement about every individual believer. I rendered it as Christ grieving over the believer’s wandering with holy compassion.

The phrase “perfect created love and the most perfect uncreated love” is theologically dense and could be misunderstood. I treated it as a reference to Christ’s truly human love and eternal divine love united in the one person of the Savior.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted “embrace thee, though I once took lust and sin in my arms” as a request for grace to turn from once-cherished sin and cling to Christ as better, rather than as a generic request for stronger religious feeling.

I rendered the Joseph-and-his-brothers comparison as Christ welcoming the sinner with joy rather than with pained reluctance. This preserves the original contrast without requiring the modern reader to know the Genesis allusion immediately.

I kept the original’s movement from the cross outward into fellowship, sun, rain, river, cleansing, and the tree of life, because the prayer is not moving away from the gospel but learning to see Christ’s love reflected through creation and final hope.
